titulo.texto: Mural “The Spiritual World of the Peninsular Maya,” by Rafael Coronel

frase_gancho.texto: A painter from Zacatecas, son-in-law of Diego Rivera, portrayed the beliefs of the Maya peninsula.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the spiritual world of Yucatán, we return to the jungle of Chiapas. Look for a long, white, unadorned tunic, like the ones Lacandon men wear.

guion_corto.texto: This painting is by Rafael Coronel, an artist born in Zacatecas in 1931 who married Ruth Rivera, daughter of the muralist Diego Rivera. In 1964, the year the museum opened, he painted two murals for its halls. This one is called “The Spiritual World of the Peninsular Maya.” The peninsular Maya are those of the Yucatán Peninsula, which today covers the states of Yucatán, Campeche and Quintana Roo. The museum commissioned murals from several artists to help visitors understand each culture, and Coronel was assigned this hall. Its title speaks of what cannot be seen: the beliefs, the gods and the ceremonies of a people who are still very much alive. After the house and the [Maya homestead](mna_s19_solar_maya), the mural invites you to look at what lies behind daily life.

guion_largo.texto:
How do you paint something that cannot be seen? That is the question raised by the title of this mural: “The Spiritual World of the Peninsular Maya.” It does not say “house,” or “costume,” or “cornfield,” which are things you can touch. It speaks of gods, of prayers and of ceremonies. It is a mural that asks you to look with different eyes.

It was painted by Rafael Coronel, born in Zacatecas on October twenty-fourth, 1931. He arrived in Mexico City in 1951, studied architecture at UNAM and later painting at La Esmeralda. In 1960 he married Ruth Rivera, daughter of Diego Rivera, and that is why he is called the son-in-law of the great muralist. But he built his own fame: he is remembered above all for his portraits. He died in 2019.

Coronel had another passion, masks. In Zacatecas, in the former convent of San Francisco, stands the museum that bears his name. It holds a collection of Mexican masks, used in festivals and rituals from all over the country, which is considered one of the largest in the world. According to what is told, the museum was born to house the collection that the painter himself gathered. Someone who brought together so many masks knew the festivals and popular beliefs of Mexico very closely.

In 1964, the year of the opening, murals were commissioned from several artists for the different halls, with an educational purpose. This is recorded in the catalog of the works of art of that year, prepared by the historian Justino Fernández. You have already seen some of them: the [stained-glass window by Carlos Mérida](mna_s13_vitral_goeritz), in the Gran Nayar hall, and the Purépecha wedding by Pablo O’Higgins. Right here, in this hall, is the magical world of [Leonora Carrington](mna_s19_mural_carrington). Coronel painted two: this one and another titled “Abstraction.”

The word “peninsular” points to a geography. The Yucatán Peninsula is a flat land of limestone, with few rivers, where water is kept in cenotes and in wells. That is why the rain god, Chaac, is so important. You have already seen his face, with its nose curled upward, in the [mask of Kabah](mna_s09_mascaron_chaac).

The title does not say what specific scene the artist painted. A good key for looking at it is the Cha Chaak, the ceremony to ask for rain that you have just learned about in the [Maya homestead](mna_s19_solar_maya) and that is still celebrated in communities of Yucatán. It is led by a Maya priest, called a jmeen, who prays in the Maya language. An altar is built of wood and leaves, with gourd bowls, candles and a cross, and foods made of corn are offered. At the end, those who took part eat together what was first offered to the gods. Look at the mural with that question in mind: do you see figures gathered together, an altar, a face that recalls Chaac?

That the Maya spiritual world is still alive is the idea behind this whole hall. In 2024, in the midst of a drought, the Cha Chaak was celebrated again in several towns of Yucatán, as a living part of agricultural faith. The spiritual is not only the past: it is a way of asking, of giving thanks and of living together with the forest, the rain and the corn.

Before moving on, go back for a moment to the house you have just seen. Inside there is a small family altar, and outside, a homestead with a garden and bees. The mural completes the picture: the house, the garden and, behind it all, a world of gods who listen.

texto: Look for figures gathered together, as in a ceremony
Look at the colors that dominate the painting and think about what you feel when you see them
Compare any face or symbol with the mask of Chaac that you saw in the Maya hall

texto.Author: Rafael Coronel (1931-2019)
texto.Work: “The Spiritual World of the Peninsular Maya”
texto.Subject: the spiritual world of the Maya of the Yucatán Peninsula

texto.pregunta: Myth: The Maya of Yucatán stopped celebrating their ceremonies centuries ago.
texto.respuesta: Reality: The Cha Chaak, a ceremony to ask for rain, is still celebrated today, led by a Maya priest who prays in the Maya language.
